We have, in the crest of the Prince of Wales, under the three white ostrich feathers, the motto ' Ich Dien '-I serve. And so honoured a place has this motto, and the idea it represents in our minds that we have the nobility of service taught in the schools. The attempt is now made to reverse that. Instead of it being a virtue to serve, it is represented as a virtue to quit. It is so important a revolution in the ethics of this country that it should be commemorated. There should be pictures of the three members filing out of the committee room with the motto, ' I quit.' The white feathers might remain, for I think they would be quite appropriate. And these should be posted in the public schools, to teach the precept hereafter that quitting is a virtue instead of service.

I do
not propose to follow my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in showing the enormous amounts of money involved in this question. I think there can be no doubt in the mind of any hon. member that the amount involved in the question whether there has been gross negligence, or whether there has been swindling in connection with these operations is enormous, it is away op in the millions. The first estimate we had of the cost of this road from the government was $51,000,000. There cannot be a doubt now that the cost will be at least three times that-probably more. So it is of great importance to the people of this Dominion that the truth should be known as to how this great discrepancy has occurred. Therefore it is that the hon. member for South Simcoe took some pains to lay before the House and the country the real gravity of the situation, that the people might understand that this is not merely a question whether three gentlemen choose, or did not choose, to go on with this inquiry, but a question whether there shall be a fair and full inquiry into a matter of great practical importance to the public.
Now, I observe that the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. A. H. Clarke) has tried to be a little humorous and sarcastic. He says that the charges made by Mr. Lumsden are against other officers lower than himself. That is nrecisely what a majority of the committee are trying to make out, the case is represented to be from first to lastr-simply a quarrel, a difference of opinion, between Mr. Lumsden and his subordinates. But no one knows better than the hon. member from South Essex that there is _ a much graver question than that in it. It has been stated in writing that these subordinate officers are believed to have been acting, not upon their own motion, but under instructions given by those above both, themselves and Mr. Lumsden. The question, therefore, arises who are the people who have led these subordinates to do these wrong actions. That is a most important question and it is the question upon which everything turns. We have not been trying to find out exactly what was the motive of the subordinate engineers. I do not believe for a moment that these subordinate engineers have been doing this off their own bat; I am quite sure they have not. Thev have known that they have the support and backing of people in place, who can maintain them and support them in whatever they do; otherwise those men, I believe, would never have done what they did. Now I do not propose to occupy the time of the House in discussing what it was necessary for my hon. friend from Simcoe to discuss; I propose to deal simply with the question why I felt compelled to withdraw from the com-

mittee when I had been, appointed to it by this House, and had accepted the position. I admit the gravity of the step that I took, I am not going to treat it lightly, and I hope the House will believe that I realized the gravity of the step. I retired because I felt it was my duty to get out of that committee, and not he a party to what I might call a whitewashing operation. That is the truth, and the whole truth. If I had had any doubt as to the propriety of my conduct, I would have been satisfied to go on. But I have no doubt now, and I had no doubt at the time; I believe now* that I was right in the course I took.
Now I want to recall for a moment the beginning of this thing. It is in the recollection of the House that in 1908 Major Hodgins, then in charge of 386 miles of the western end of this section of the road, had made grave charges against the staff, and his charges, his allegations, extended not merely to his own district F. but also to section B. Those allegations led practically to his dismissal by the commission. Subsequently a committee, known as the Hodgins Committee, of which I was a member, and two other gentlemen opposite were members, was appointed to investigate that question. I need not state what that committee did. Nothing resulted. The majority of the committee on that inquiry cleverly induced Mr. Hodgins to admit that the inquiry would be more satisfactorily prosecuted by a board of engineers than by the committee that was investigating it, and thereupon the whole thing was thrown overboard, and that was practically the end of the Hodgins inquiry. But, Mr. Speaker, within a year afterwards the whole country was startled by hearing that the chief engineer, who, acting under the	commission, had been a party to the dismissal of Mr. Hodgins, had himself resigned, and in doing so had made grave and serious charges with respect to the very districts that were involved in the Hodgins inquiry. The Hodgins inquiry arose largely on district F, but Mr. Hodgins had been taken down to what is called a kindergarten show on B, and so some evidence was given as to district B. And those two districts, F and B, are the districts with which the whole inquiry under the Lumsden Committee is concerned. We had that investigation in 1908, and no action was taken by the government, no action was taken by the commission, no investigation as to what was the real truth about the Hodgins complaints. Everything was smoothed over, not a word from the government, or from any department of the government on that subject, until Mr. Lumsden throws up his most important position, his salary of $6,000 a year, goes entirely out of the service of the commission, because he could not stand what was going on. Now that was a startling posi-
What page was that?

I will give it to my hon. friend. Then the minority saw at once the position going to be taken by the majority. There was no complaint, no charge against the commission, and they were not to be investigated. I dare say they would have objected to any investigation as against themselves, there being no charge against them, and they had the authority of the hon. member for Pictou to that effect. We never concealed our view of the position. We- said frankly: We of the minority desire to prove this case if it can be proved, and on the other hand, the hon. members comprising the majority would prefer that we should not prove it. Therefore, we said, if this is to be nrosecuted in the sense of a public prosecution and a public inquiry, we, who want to see this investigation succeed, should have the nomination of counsel and not those who want to see it fail. I think that was a perfectly legitimate position to take, and we were driven to it by the fact that Mr. Lumsden had refused to have any counsel, for in the absence of counsel representing the minority or Mr. Lumsden there would have been no prosecution of the inquiry at all. A motion was made by us that we should not proceed until counsel had been appointed. Immediately afterwards the suggestion was made that the hon. member for Pictou and I should meet and endeavour to agree upon counsel. We did meet, and ultimately we failed to agree upon counsel. The hon. member for Pictou said to me-there is nothing private in what I shall state-'Suppose we (the majority) name a Conservative lawyer of high standing'? I replied : 'It does not matter at all whom you name; our position is that you are not to name the man to prosecute this inquiry, but that he should be named by us because we desire the prosecution of the inquiry.' That position was taken fairly and squarely. There is no question about the position that we represented. We said: No matter how eminent the counsel may be, if he be nominated by the majority he will regard himself as acting for them, while if we nominate him, he will know that, and accept our directions and act on our behalf. I see it has been asserted that we did not

name any counsel. I rather gathered from the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Clarke) that he was under the impression that we did not name counsel. I named three counsel to the hon. member for Pictou and not one of them was satisfactory to him. I do not find fault with him for it, but I did name three, and I venture to say that the counsel I named were quite as eminent, quite as well known as the gentlemen they have appointed, and probably more broadly known throughout Canada. But .just consider what the objection was. The minority were content to have certain gentlemen as counsel. The hon. member for Pictou did not think them eminent enough. Surely, if we, who were really anxious to succeed in this inquiry, were satisfied with the counsel, he need not have made much objection. We were the parties who wanted the work well done, we were the side that wanted the eminent counsel, and we were not likely to take a man who would not have done his work well. We knew the men perhaps as well as the hon. member for Pictou did. But nothing would satisfy him, and the hon. member will recollect that our endeavours to agree upon a counsel ended by his telling me that they had decided to stand by Mr. Wallace Nesbitt. That ended it, and there was no use in proceeding further on that subject. I do not propose to mention the names of the other gentlemen. They have not been appointed, and privately we agreed that we would not mention the names of any who were not appointed. There is not the same objection to mentioning the name of Mr. Wallace Nesbitt, because his name has been published in the press, and Mr. Chrysler has been appointed, so that the same secrecy is not called for with reference to these gentlemen. But the other gentlemen would have been quite satisfactory to us, and if we were satisfied with them, I don't see why the majority should have objected. As to Mr. Nesbitt, I wish to say, as the member for Simcoe said, that there was no question at all about his standing or his professional reputation or anything of that kind. He is a personal friend of mine. We made no question about his ability, but what we did say was that we would not have Mr. Nesbitt or any other man who was the nominee of the majority of that committee. We made that perfectly plain; there is no doubt at all about it; our objection was that we knew that neither Mr. Nesbitt or any other gentleman named by the majority could do the duty we required of him to probe that matter to the bottom. If the majority of the committee appointed him he would know for whom he was acting, and if we nominated him he would know he was acting for us. That is all we eared for, and Mr. BARKER.
we laid that principle down, and the majority refused to assent to it. The position we took was made perfectly clear, because I drew up a short memorandum in the nature of a report and submitted it to my friends in the minority, and it was read and appears on the minutes. It was to this effect:
Mr. Chairman,-Pursuant to what passed at rhe last meeting, Mr. Macdonald and 1 endeavoured to agree upon counsel to act in the prosecution of this investigation. We have failed to agree. I insisted that the members of this committee who represent the opposition should nominate that counsel, subject, of course, to the gentleman named being a proper person, acceptable in that regard to the committee.
We did not wish to bring in any man, regardless of his standing and we conceded that he must be a man of character and standing at the bar. Subject to it being approved in that respect, we claimed that the man who was going to pursue that inquiry to the end ought to act for us and be named by us.
Mr, Macdonald would not concede that we of the opposition should have such nomination. We have therefore failed to agree, and f may at once say that that question was the real difficulty. I am not now arguing the question but stating the facts, and to put my position clearly I move:-
That it is the right and duty of the members of this committee who represent the opposition to nominate a counsel who shall prosecute this investigation in the public interest.
The majority voted down that resolution, four to three.
Now, I have endeavoured to make quite clear what it is that we contended for-the commissioners were represented by counsel selected by themselves and paid by_ the country; Mr. Lumsden took the position that he was simply a witness, th*t he was ready to answer as a witness, but that ha was not prosecuting and would not /appoint counsel to make good his charges. It was not disputed that there ought to be counsel to prosecute the inquiry and establish the charges if they were true. _ The only question was who should nominate that counsel; should he be nominated by the opposition members, whose interests and whose wishes, were to probe the matter to the very root, or, by the government majority on the committee, who, as we said, and as we believed, would desire and prefer that the charges should fail. There was the clear issue, and there could not be any question about that. There was no misunderstanding about it at all. We wanted a counsel to act for Us who knew that he was acting for us and for nobody else; we wanted him to know that he was not acting for the government, because the government would be blameahle if the charges

were driven home; we wanted him to know that he was not acting for the commis sion, because they had their own counsel, and they would be to blame if the charges were driven home. We contended that in the	public	interest there shouldbe counsel who would follow np every charge	to	the	end and endeavour	tomake	it	good,	if it were possible	tomake	it	good.	But the majority	of
the committee scoffed at our want of faith in them; our want of faith in the absolute purity of their motives. One after the -other of them read us homilies upon partisanship; they all professed there was nothing like partisanship on their side, and that they were above that sort of thing. I recollect that one member of the majority of that committee-I need not mention his name-was so horrified by the doubts cast by the member for Simcoe upon their perfect impartiality, that he exclaimed: My God, what do you want? and he added: I am an honest man.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Hear, hear.

Well, they were all honourable men, of course, but they recognized us three of the minority as partisans, and they themselves: Oh, no, they were not partisans. But we frankly treated ' them as partisans. We wanted to drive that case home, and wTe said so, and wa said we wanted counsel to help us in doing it. We represented that we did not want the other side to appoint their own counsel to prove them guilty. We knew they would not do it, and we did not propose to go through the humbugging operation of having a counsel to defeat the objects of the men whom he was supposed to be working for.
I want to say a few words moTe. I have already said that Mr. Nesbitt is a friend of mine, but that does not debar me from saying a fe\s words as to the impropriety of any attempt to get him to act as counsel. I put that squarely. I will read a few letters from the Hodgin's inquiry. At page 420 of that inquiry there is this letter:
Toronto, November 27, 1907.
P. E. Ryan, Esq.,
Secretary of Board of Commissioners of Transcontinental Railway,
Ottawa.
Sir,-We have obtained the opinion of Mr. allace Nesbitt, K.C., on the interpretation of clauses 34, 35 and 36 of the specifications, and will forward same to you by to-morrow's mail, and have the honour to remain,
Your obedient servants,

MOSS & THOMPSON.
I may say that clauses 34 and 35 and 36 of the specifications referred to in this letter are the basis of all the trouble. There is another letter on page 421 which reads:
Toronto, November 28, 1907.
P. E. Ryan, Esq.,
Secretary of the Board of Commisioners of the Transcontinental Railway,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-Re contract for the construction of the Transcontinental railway (eastern division) and specifications attached thereto.
We have the honour to inclose you herewith the opinion of Mr. Wallace Nesbitt, K.C., as to the construction to be placed upon the language used in the above specifications in the classification of material. Kindly acknowledge.
We have the honour to remain, Sir,
Your obedient servants,

MOSS & THOMPSON.
Then there is this letter from the secretary of the Transcontinental Railway Commission to the Minister of Railways:
Ottawa, December 2, 1907.
Sir,-I have the honour, by direction 9f the Board, to hand you, which I do herewith, a letter from Mr. Wallace Nesbitt. K.C., addressed to Messrs. Macdonald & O'Brien, and submitted on their behalf to the commissioners, containing Mr. Nesbitt's opinion as to the construction to be placed upon the language used in the specifications with respect to the classification of material; and I am to request that you will have this letter placed on the file which accompanied my letter to you ot the 23rd ult. and considered therewith.
1 have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,

Secretary.
Then follows a very long letter from Mr. Nesbitt, K.C., to Macdonald & O'Brien, contractors on district B, discussing these questions of classification that the witnesses are to be examined upon; that Mr. Lumsden is being examined upon; that Mr Smith, the counsel for the commission, is doing his best to break him down upon. All these are discussed by Mr. Nesbitt, and that letter of his was filed as evidence in the Hodgin's inquiry, and Mr. Nesbitt commits himself to opinions on this classification diametrically opposed to Mr. Hodgin's views and to those of Mr. Lumsden. Just picture Mr. Nesbitt acting in this inquiry and putting in Mr. Nesbitt's written letter as evidence to prove what the true construction and meaning of the specifications was. What position would we have occupied if we had agreed to accept Mr. Nesbitt to prosecute this investigation, and he had been asked by the unanimous committee to take the brief? Perhaps Mr. Nesbitt would have accepted the brief under such conditions, but when he heard that we objected to anybody named by the majority, he at once declined. And yet we were asked to accept him as the one man who above all others could do his duty in this matter. I know Mr. Nesbitt well, and we all have the highest respect for him, but I repeat that no-

man could do his duty in prosecuting this investigation who had given that opinion He was against Mr. Lumsden from the word go, and he could not do his duty from our point of view. He would have done his duty according to the opinion of the majority of the committee, 1 have no doubt. I do not like to say that they deliberately selected him knowing that, but it is most extraordinary that even in this Lumsden inquiry that very opinion has been put in evidence against Mr. Lumsden, as already published by this very majority.
Does my hon. friend say that the question on which Mr. Nesbitt gave the opinion is the issue now before the committee?
I say that the specifications as to rock, loose rock, and common excavation are dealt with in that opinion broadly and largely, and these are the very questions coming up.
My hon. friend does not follow the question I was asking. I want to know whether he says that the matter referred to in that opinion is the issue before this committee.

I say that after the Hod-gins inquiry Air. Lumsden consented to certain variations, but the man who gave that opinion could not have an unbiassed mind on the question between Afr. Lumsden, and the contractors.
Mr. AfACDONALD. Why not?

Well, I would rather not employ him if I had a case against the contractors.
Afr. AfACDONALD. If my hon. friend is not prepared to say that the opinion of Mr. Nesbitt is on the question at issue before this committee, there is no reason why he should not have been employed.
I assume that it is in issue, or they would not have put it in in evidence in this very case.
It might have been evidence, and not in issue.
It could not have been evidence unless in issue.

It bears on the case, and the man who gave that opinion would not have been in a position to act as a proper counsel against the government, or against the contractors.
I want to recall to the memory of this House a case that arose when hon. gentlemen were in the minority, and the Conservatives were in power, and I want to contrast the treatment that was accorded to them with the treatment that the government to-day Mr. BARKER.
are according to the opposition. The cases are very much alike. I refer to the celebrated McGreevy case of 1891. Allegations of misdoing had been made by a brother of Afr. McGreevy, involving not only him, and certain contractors, but also the Minister and Department of Public Works of that day. Sir John A. Macdonald was the leader of the government, and I think Sir John Thompson was Minister of Justice. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) was then in opposition, and Mr. Tarte, a member of the Liberal opposition, presented to the House a resolution demanding an inquiry before a special committee. It was suggested that it might go before the Committee on Privileges and Elections, which was assented to on all sides. I need hardly say that the majority on that, committee were Conservatives, and the minority, including the right hon. gentleman, Mr. Tarte, and others, were Liberals in opposition. It appears that at the first meeting of the committee Mr. Tarte appeared with counsel, who was Mr. Geoffrion, K.C., a brother of the chairman of this Lumsden committee, a fact which might have recalled to him the history of the AfcGreevy case. No objection was made at all. There was no pretense on the part of the partisan Conservative majority that they should name the counsel to prosecute the inquiry-not a word on that subject. Mr. Geoffrion acted as counsel, and was paid by the government of the day. I do not suppose he was paid in advance; he was paid afterwards, I believe, $3,000. But the point I make is that while the right hon. gentleman, then in opposition, was willing to accept from the Conservative majority of that committee what he refuses to us, he claims that he is all right now, and I suppose he was all right then-he wants to take both sides. He was glad to accept from Sir John Macdonald the privilege of appointing counsel to investigate that case, but he refuses to give the minority in this case the privilege which he enjoyed in the AfcGreevy case. Why is it so? Counsel were appointed in that case for the Public Works Department, an analogous appointment to that of Mr. Smith for the commission. Those prosecuting the charges were allowed counsel named by themselves and the government paid him. Counsel were appointed for the contractors. The contractors paid their own counsel, but all others were paid by the government. It appears that there were a hundred meetings of that committee, and it is stated in the speech with which the report was made that in all those hundred metings there wa3 only one division of the committee. And on that occasion, with a majority of Conservatives in the House, the motion

was carried two to one, showing that the conservatives supported the opposition of that day in what they wanted. Not only that but it was said there, and uncontradicted, that the utmost freedom was given in the production of evidence. In one. case in which a witness refused to hand a book over to the committee, the Liberal members wanted possession of the book, so as to examine every page of it. The witness said he would let them see everything relating to the case, but not the whole book. The matter was brought before the House, and Sir John Thompson himself, moved a resolution that the witness be compelled to hand the book over to the committee, and he was compelled to do so. Just look on the two pictures. There is what the Conservative government did. Contrast that with the refusal of thi3 government to allow the minority to nominate, counsel.
Did the hon. gentleman ever make a charge as Mr. Tarte did?
Mr. Tarte simply took up what was published. Mr. McGreevy's brother was charging him with certain wrong doing. Mr. Tarte brought the matter before the House, and a committee was granted at once.
Did not Mr. Tarte come before the committee with his own counsel? The committee did not appoint his counsel.
He acted for the minority all through and was paid $3,000 by the government.
Did Mr. Tarte not come to the committee with his own counsel and ask the committee to allow his counsel to appear for him?
He simply came there with his counsel. The next day he explained to the committee that his counsel was absent owing to illness in his family.
Did not Mr. Tarte make the charges on his responsibility as a member of this House? And if he had not succeeded in establishing them, would he not have had to resign his position?

There is no such law as that. What difference did it make here? If the right hon. the leader of the government had not moved the resolution he did would not the leader of the oposition have moved it. Do you suppose that the resignation of Mr. Lumsden would have been allowed to go without inquiry? If the right hon. gentleman had not moved for a committee, a committee would have been moved for from this side of the House. What difference would it make?

If my hon. friend will look at the report of the proceedings of the committee referred to, he will see that the chairman, Mr. Girouard, having asked whether any of the parties desired to be heard by counsel, Mr. Tarte handed him the name of Mr. C. A. Geoffrion. It was Mr. Tarte who appointed his own counsel, and not the committee at all.

We can easily get counsel if you will allow him to act, but you will have no counsel. The government of that day paid Mr. Tarte's counsel. Mr. Tarte was only one member of that committee and his request was granted. But three-fourths of the committee in the present case have asked for counsel and their request is refused?

Did not Mr. Tarte
have his counsel appointed because he made the charge?

Mr. Tarte went there with his counsel, and the chairman of the committee asked him if he wanted to appear by counsel, and Mr. Tarte said he did. Why could not that be done here? On the Lumsden Committee, there were three members of that committee who wanted to appoint counsel, and their request was refused.
If my hon. friend had made any charges himself, no doubt, he would have got his counsel, but he did not make any charges, and Mr. Lumsden said he did not want any counsel.
Suppose I had moved that resolution, would it have made any difference whether it was moved by me instead of the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the case alluded to, Mr. Tarte made an accusation which put in peril the seat of two members of the House, Mr. McGreevy and Mr. Langevin.
How would it imperil Mr. Tarte's seat?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the charges were proved, he would be unworthy of a seat in this House.
There is no such law in England or Canada.
The right hon. gentleman will not contend that it is absolute law that a man who fails to prove his charge will lose his seat.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not say it is statutory law but it has been the law of parliament.
Never.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was not Mr. Sadler expelled from parliament on a charge against him?
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said that Mr. Tarte *would have lost his seat if he had not been able to make his charges good.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, and I say it on the authority of Sir John Macdonald. When in the Pacific scandal Mr. Huntingdon made a charge against Sir John Macdonald, Sir John said that Mr. Huntingdon would be driven out of the House if, having made such charges as he did, he failed to prove them. No doubt if the charges were not true, Mr. Huntingdon would have been unworthy of a seat in this House.

Sir John Thompson at the time certain charges were made by Mr. Edgar, reviewed the whole question and declared that, having carefully examined the cases, there was absolutely no such rule in parliament.

You will find on inquiry that the law is this. There is no penalty against any member making a charge against a fellow member involving the loss of his seat as the consequence of a failure to prove the charge; but if the charges are of such a character that, not being proved, the House considered that the member who made them is not a fit and proper person to sit among gentlemen, the House will expel him.

In that case the man would be guilty of conduct not becoming a gentleman. But that is not the point here. In the Tarte case, Mr. Tarte took up matters of public rumour and put them into the form of a resolution, and a committee was granted without discussion. He went before the committee and brought counsel with him, without permission of the committee or anybody else.
He was not a member of the Committee on Privileges and Elections at that time.
I think he was. I do not think that that committee is confined even now to members of the legal profession. At all events, I have seen his name in that committee.
He was at their meeting.

He was in the list of members oif the committee. There are members on that committee now who are not lawyers. It has been the general understanding that on that committee lawyers should be appointed, but there are members on it who are not lawyers. It may be that his name was put down by ^ Mr. BARKER,
mistake, but it was there. I know the right hon. gentleman was there-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No; I was a
member of the committee, but I did not attend on that occasion; I took no part at all.

The hon. member's name was down as being present. However, there was the position-it seems perfectly clear that the right hon. gentleman was glad to accept the privilege granted Mr. Tarte of appearing by counsel to prosecute the inquiry, but that he refused to allow the minority in this case, when they asked for it, the same privilege. I do not understand how that can be justified except on the ground of brute majority. There is no other reason for it.
I do not like that expression ' brute majority.' Perhaps the hon. member might use some other.

I do not use it in a personal sense. But,* in any case, I do not wish to insist upon it. What I insist upon is that in a matter of this importance, involving so much to this country, it is an outrage upon public rights for the government to refuse the appointment of counsel to represent the prosecution in this ca.se, and that the investigation should be going on in the way it is without any counsel there to drive home the charges against the commission or the government,
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

When my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) was speaking, I was surprised to hear a gentleman of his eminence at the bar quoting a part of the evidence, and discussing it when the whole of that evidence is not yet adduced before the committee, just as if he were taking evidence before a lower court, and reporting it to a higher tribunal before all the evidence was taken. Now the question may be fairly reduced to this, whether my hon. friends opposite were logical, and rational in withdrawing from the committee on the sole ground that they had not the exclusive choice of counsel. That question of choosing a counsel was first submitted, I think they will admit, and pressed by themselves. Although I agreed with them that perhaps it would be better to have counsel, I had my doubts whether the committee, composed as it was of eminent lawyers, at least six members on the committee were eminent lawyers, could not themselves take charge of the investigation. In other committees, for instance in the Public Accounts Committee, the cus-

tom is for some one of the members to take charge of a particular case, and conduct it himself. I did not see why the members of this committee could not conduct the investigation themselves. However, it was thought proper for the speedy conduct of the proceedings to appoint a counsel. Then the question arose whether the counsel should be appointed by the whole committee or by the three members composing the minority. We submitted to them that it was only fair that the whole committee, representing as it did the whole people, should appoint the counsel. They would not admit that proposition, they contended that they alone should have the exclusive right to appoint ia counsel. We had before us the precedent of the Hodgins investigation. The gentleman who made the charge in that case came before the committee accompanied with his counsel. In this case the circumstances were very much the same. The charges were made, not by members of the opposition, but by Mr. Lumsden himself against some of his subordinate engineers. It was certainly the right, a right always acknowledged by other such committees, that the parties interested might appear before the committee accompanied by their own counsel. We all expected that Mr. Lumsden would come before that committee with counsel, we also expected that the commission would come accompanied by counsel; it was fair also that the engineers against whom charges had been made, should be represented by counsel. Then the question arose whether the committee itself should be represented by counsel, and we thought that the minority members of the committee were not fair in asking that they alone should be entrusted with the choice of counsel. Hon. gentlemen who have read the report will see that the matter was left to two members of the committee, Mr. Macdonald, and Mr. Barker, to decide who should be appointed. In all the discussions that arose between_ the members of the committee, ' the majority contended that they had just as much right to submit names as the minority. Of course we did not wish to appoint a gentleman who was in active politics, we admitted that it would not be fair to the minority to take a man who was engaged in party strife; but we thought it would be fair to take a man of high reputation at the bar, a man who had the confidence of the whole country, and who was not known to be a politician. We went further, and we offered to submit to them a gentleman who belonged to their own party; but still they insisted that they alone should have the right to appoint a counsel. That was their contention, and they would not depart from it. We could not agree with them, and I am ready to submit our view of the matter to the judg-193
ment of the House, and to the judgment of the people at large.
Now,_ reference has several times been made in this discussion to the McGreevy affair as a precedent. At that time I happened to be a partner with my brother, Mr. C. A. Geoffrion, who was appointed counsel by Mr. Tarte. Mr. Tarte made the charge himself, he chose his own counsel. He came to the office when I was present, and engaged my brother, and agreed to pay him himself. Mr. Geoffrion accordingly came before the committee, and took charge of the whole matter for Mr. Tarte, for the man who had made the charges. After proceedings had been going on before the committee for a little time, parliament thought proper to pay themselves the counsel that had been named by Mr. Tarte. Now we did exactly the same thing in the Hodgins case. Mr. Hodgins, who had made the charges, came before the committee accompanied by his counsel. Hie committee admitted that he had thes right to be represented by counsel, and we recommended to the House that the House should pay his counsel. We did just what was done by the House in the McGreevy case, when it paid Mr. Tarte's counsel. And if Mr. Lumsden had chosen to come before the committee with his own counsel, doubtless the House would have consented to pay his counsel, as it did in the cases of Mr. Tarte and Major Hodgins.
Now, Sir, I do not think that the minority members of the committee were really acting fairly when they contended that they were not well treated. They admitted themeslves that they were prejudiced in the matter, they cannot deny it, it is in the report. They say that both parties are prejudiced. We would not admit that, we no more desired to see Mr. Lumsden fail in his charges than we desired to see the engineers fail in their defence, the men who were employees of the commission and consequently employees of the government. Why should we? We took the ground that all members of the committee were disposed to probe the matter to the bottom. If the engineers had done anything wrong we wanted to discover it, in order that we might advise the committee, and advise the House. On the other hand, if Mr. Lumsden fails in proving his charges so much the worse for him. No doubt hon. gentlemen opposite are desirous of finding that the charges made by Mr. Lumsden against the engineers are true.
I have been chairman of the committee, and I think that hon. gentlemen will admit that I have treated everybody as fairly as I could. I have done my very best to help everybody. The committee recommended that Mr. Chrysler put himself in communication with Mr. Lumsden. We advised Mr. Lumsden to tell him every-

thing he could and to come and report to the committee if anything was wrong, assuring him that anything that was wrong would be remedied. As far as Mr. Chrysler is concerned, I had dealings with him as a lawyer before I came to this House,' and I had dealings as against him in certain cases. I always found him a very eminent lawyer, a man jealous of his reputation, and I cannot conceive of Mr. Chrysler not doing everything to probe this matter to the bottom in face of the instructions given to him that he must do his very best in that direction. Mr. Lumsden is there to give him all the assistance possible. The commission is open to Mr. Chrysler and Mr. Lumsden, they can go to the books and find out anything they desire to know and produce the evidence before the committee. I do not see why my hon. friends opposite are opposed to the appointment of Mr. Chrysler. The hon. member for South Sim-coe went so far as to insinuate that Mr. Chrysler's standing in the profession was not of the highest. I think that all parties before the committee are well represented. Mr. Smith stands at the top of his profession in the province of Quebec. Mr. Moss is an eminent lawyer, and I think Mr. Chrysler is in the first rank of his profession. But, if my hon. friends opposite desired at heart to investigate this matter properly, why did they not themselves undertake to do it? They are three eminent lawyers well able to conduct the investigation themselves. Any one of them could have taken charge of the investigation. In fact, we do not need any lawyer. Any one of them could have taken charge of the investigation with the help of the other members of the committee, and it would have gone just as well perhaps as with a lawyer. But, they would not do that, and if they are not satisfied with Mr. Chrysler, why do they not come back to the committee and help to put the questions if they think that the questions are not being properly put? If they can think of anything else, they are welcome to come before the committee and ask questions, as they have a right to do. I do not think we need to extend this discussion. As I said in the beginning, this is not the place or the time to discuss the question of the cost of the Transcontinental railway, and it is not the time to discuss the evidence. I do not think the House has the right to discuss the evidence, because it is not before them I do not think it is fair or rational that any member of this House should take the evidence and discuss it when it is not all before the committee yet, and when members of the engineering staff have not been examined. My hon. friend from South Simcoe this afternoon took some parts of the evidence, commented upon them, and left other parts, which, in some instances, contradict those parts which he was commenting upon. I submit that the commit-Mr. GEOFFRION.
tee is acting fairly, that it is trying to do its best, and that the House and the people may have every confidence that it will do its duty.

There is scarcely a question dealt with byt this House, or by any of its committees, which is not approached and determined from a party standpoint, and the one before us now is assuredly not one of the exceptions. Conduct and transactions are approved of in this House, which, disassociated from party politics, would receive the prompt condemnation of every rightthinking man. The report under consideration, for the first time, raises the question why the minority on the Lums-der. committee refused longer to participate in the investigation, and for the first time gives them an opportunity of answering that question, which, like all other questions, has two sides.
Those who approve the action of the majority on the Lumsden Investigation Committee, try to justify it in this way. They say that Mr. Lumsden, in June last, when resigning his position as chief engineer of the National Transcontinental railway, gave as his reason for so doing, that he had lost confidence in some of the engineers for improper classification and measurements of construction work in sections ' B ' and ' F '; that, recently, at the instance of the government, the House authorized them to appoint a select committee of seven to investigate the charge thus made, which was accordingly done, four supporters of the government and three members of the opposition being chosen; that the government and its supporters have no desire or interest to serve other than to ascertain whether the charge be well founded; that on behalf of the people they seek the truth merely; that no charge against the government is made, and therefore it is not a party matter at all; that the whole people of Canada being interested counsel chosen to conduct the investigation should have a national reputation for ability and probity, and should be selected by a majority of the committee, namely, by the four government supporters on it; that they having chosen such a man, the minority on the committee should be satisfied, and that it was unreasonable and unprecedented that they should insist on being permitted to name counsel.
That, I think, is a fair statement of the attitude taken by the majority on the committee, and supported by their political friends-plausible, but, as it seems to me fallacious as well.
Let us, for a moment, examine the other view of the situation as taken by the minority. The government undertook to construct the National Transcontinental railway, to construct that part of it between Winnipeg and Moncton directly as a government work. The government, therefore,

is responsible to the people of Canada for the manner in which that great work is being done, more especially that part of it. When taking power to build that part of the road, they told the people that they had all the requisite information to enable them to say that it could be built for $51,300,000. The work of construction has now proceeded sufficiently far to enable them to admit that it will probably cost at least three times the sum so named. That admission naturally suggests either that they had not comprehensive and reliable information when those figures were given, or that they are paying for the work enormously more than it is fairly worth. And the reason given by Mr. Lumsden for his resignation points to the latter.
As already stated, the government is strictly and fully responsible to parliament and to the people, in every particular, for the manner in which the great project is being prosecuted, for the conduct of every one engaged in the prosecution thereof, whether it be that of the chief engineer, of the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners, or of the resident and district engineers.
It therefore follows that the investigation directed by this House, and limited as it is to sections ' B ' and ' F ' of the road- although the opposition contended it should cover the whole project-places the government on trial respecting the manner in which the construction so limited has thus far proceeded. Full comprehension of the above would go far to illuminate the conduct of the majority of the committee as hereinafter set forth. Further, on the 25th of June last the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners sent a letter to Mr. Lumsden, and to each of the other two arbitrators appointed to determine questions of classification, &c., which was in part as follows:
The commissioners object to and protest against proceedings of the arbitrators as being improper and illegal for the following reasons, viz.:-
(a)	That they were based in whole or in part on the said draft agreement of May 14, 1909, which had been rejected and which had no existence in fact;
(b)	That the examination of the work was of a hasty, insufficient and superficial character ;
(c)	That the engineers on the line who classified the work were not afforded a sufficient hearing and an opportunity of presenting evidence;
(d)	That the contractors were not afforded an opportunity of showing cause, and further to say that the commissioners insist in the public interest that the proceedings of the arbitration tribunal shall he exhaustive, final and conclusive; shall cover all the objections filed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and that the report of the arbitrators when made shall he supported by substantial evidence, including details of quantities, etc.
That letter clearly shows the feelings entertained by the commissioners towards Mr. Lumsden. Of that grossly improper letter, written obviously in sympathy with the subordinate engineers and contractors, and apparently to intimidate the arbitrators in the impartial discharge of their duties, the government expressed no disapproval, although it loudly called for sharp repri mand if not for immediate dismissal. The non-action of the government on that letter, and its prompt acceptance of Mr. Lumsden's resignation, show that the government determined to stand by the commissioners, their appointees, and the contractors as against Mr. Lumsden, and the people. One may pause to ask why, and receive some ugly answers to the query. The government being on trial as aforesaid, and in the light of the circumstances I have mentioned it is clear what it desires the outcome of this investigation to be, and it has taken good care to place on the committee a majority of its own supporters upon whom it can rely to guide the inquiry to a satisfactory conclusion. The railway commissioners appeared before the committee with counsel who had evidently been instructed that the carriage of the proceedings was to be in his hands, for he said:
Allow me to say one word. Of course I do not propose to apoligize for my presence here at all, hut I did imagine that I represented the public interest. But if in the course of the investigation I can help the committee in a humble way in getting at the facts my instructions are to make the inquiry within the scope of the reference as full as possible, in order to fix the responsibility, if any exists,.
But upon its being pointed out that his clients were clearly in the position of defendants, and that it would be too absurd and transparent to entrust the prosecution to the defendents counsel, the committee upon the urgency of the minority thereof determined that other counsel should be engaged to take the carriage of the investigation. >Now, it is perfectly clear Mr. Speaker, that the idea of the other members of the committee was that Mr. Smith who appeared before the committee as representing the commissioners, should have the carriage of the investigation, and that there should be no other counsel, and no counsel at all on behalf of the people. At page 11 of the evidence you will find that the hon. member for Pictou stated distinctly that the commissioners were not on trial.

The commissioners are not on trial here and there is no use of your saying so.
And further he said
Would my hon. friend quote what Mr. Lennox said right there?
I have given you the page, and the words you used.
What did Mr. Lennox say?
I am going to give more of what you said. You can give us what Mr. Lennox said. But I have no objection to giving what Mr. Lennox said. He said:

The commission is responsible for the class of engineers that they employ, to employ competent and honest engineers. The commission may he able to show that they are absolutely blameless in this matter.
That is what Mr. Lennox said, and I may say here that the chief engineer was appointed by the government, and not by the commission, under section 10 of the Transcontinental Railway Act, and under section 11 the subordinate engineers, and all other servants, and workmen are employed by the commissioners. Mr. Macdonald said in reply to Mr. Lennox:
The commissioners are not on trial here and there is no use in your saying so.

It will be just as well for us to give each member of the committee the liberty to express his ideas in his own way. Mr. Macdonald usually claims that privilege for himself, and I will take the same liberty.

That is so, and I hope I am not interferring with the expression of your views in that way, but when you say the Transcontinental Commission is on trial here I say they are not..
Well, the Transcontinental Commissioners were there with their able counsel. They were either there as defendants or as prosecutors. Mr. Macdonald repeated that they were not there as defendants, and it therefore follows that they were there as prosecutors. And, the proposition was by the four government supporters on the committee. and by the Transcontinental Commissioners, that their counsel was to have the carriage of the proceeding ..acting as prosecuting counsel as well as counsel for the defence. That is borne out by some statements made by the chairman of the committee. At page 12 there is a little conversation with the chairman which shows the view that he entertained at this stage. I quote from the evidence:

Yes, and the other side I think will desire to show that they are well founded. A lawyer will know well enough, Mr. Macdonald and Mr. Wilson will know, that no lawyer can represent two sides of a question and represent it properly. We all know that the truth can best he brought out if there is an examination, an examiner-inchief, and a cross-examiner. That is the principle of all investigations. 1 have had something to do with investigations myself, and I always encourage the appointment of counsel by any one who wished to have a re-Mr. MACDONALD.
presentative, in order to bring out the truth. We cannot help it, there are two sides upon any point, those on the one side striving in one direction and those on the other side striving in the other direction. No one lawyer can bring it all out, we understand that, and it is necessary in the interests of the public that we should have counsel on each side.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think this is a very peculiar position. There are two sides as Mr. Crothers says; I understand that one side is Mr. Lumsden making a charge against other parties, and the other side is the other parties who are accused by Mr. Lumsden. We aslc Mr. Lumsden if he wants any counsel and he says: ' No, I do not want any counsel/ Now, who is the other party? The other side is the parties who are accused by Mr. Lumsden of having disobeyed his orders. Now, if they are here and want to be represented by counsel, I, for one, see no reason why their request should not be complied with. In that case we would undoubtedly have both sides represented. On the one hand is Mr. Lumsden making the charge and on the other hand the parties who are accused if they both want to be represented by counsel I should be delighted for them to have as many counsel as they choose. That is the way I understand it, but of course I am in the hands of the committee about that.
I do not know how we can now go on and assign counsel to anybody who is not in the case. I do not think that the government, the commission or anybody else are parties to the case, except Mr. Lumsden on the one hand and the engineers accused by him on the other. That is the way I understand the case stands.
So that the chairman of this committee and the other three supporters of the gov-ment on the committee regarded the two parties in the case as Mr. Lumsden on the one hand and the subordinate engineers on the other hand, while the people of Canada had no interest whatever. On the same page Mr. Smith is reported to have said:	.
Allow me to say one word. Of course, I do not propose to apologize for my presence here at all, but I did imagine that I represented the public interest. No charge has been preferred against the commission, but the commission desires as full inquiry as possible in order to fix the responsibility if these charges are well founded, and to fix the responsibility for these unfortunate things that exist; and while I should be delighted that counsel should represent any other interests, or should represent Mr. Lumsden's interests, to which I am not objecting in the least, I must say that I have not conceived it my duty to come here to defend the commission against any charges, because I am not aware that any charges have been preferred against them. But if in the course of the investigation I can help the committee in a humble way in getting at the facts, ray instructions are to make the inquiry, within the scope of the reference, as full as possible in order to fix the responsibility if any exists.
Mr. Barker said:
As I understand Mr. Smith, he considers himself appointed by the commission to repre-

sen! the interests of the public; I, for one, as a member of the committee, think that would be narrowing very much this inquiry.
Then we have Mr. Wilson's view:
I understand that Mr. Lumsden has made some charges, or some reflections against some engineers, and I, for one, will be delighted if Mr, Lumsden is represented by counsel, and that the party or parties against whom he has laid complaints be also represented, but when you talk about counsel to represent ' the public,' that seems to me a very vague word.
So that the idea of the chairman of the committee and the other three supporters of the government on it was that Mr. Smith, who was there representing ithe commissioners, who were clearly in the position of defendants, having appointed the engineers against whom the charges were made was a proper person to undertake the carriage of the proceedings, which I think will strike any fair-minded man, any lawyer or any layman, as being a most extraordinary position for any one to take, much less for gentlemen who are members of the honourable profession to which I have the honour of belonging. Up until the third meeting of the committee our friends insisted that Mr. Lumsden should be sworn and proceed to give testimony without any other counsel being appointed. We insisted that the proper time to appoint counsel on behalf of the public was at the very beginning of the inquiry, before Mr. Lumsden or any other witness was called to give testimony. When it was announced that Mr. Lumsden was not to have counsel for himself we made a motion to adjourn in order that we might consider the question of naming counsel for the other side; but that resolution of ours was voted down, and the majoritv of the committee insisted that Mr. Lumsden, the chief witness for the prosecution, should proceed to give his testimony without any lawyer to represent the public, and that was carried. Afterwards the hon. member for Pictou admitted that counsel ought to be appointed to represent the other side, and at page 75 made quite lengthy remarks in reference to that. He said:
Mr. Lumsden says, ' I am not going to be a prosecutor in this matter at all; I am not going to bring counsel; I don't want counsel; I am here only as a witness.' He disclaims any responsibility of any character whatever; consequently the committee would be left in this position, with the assistance of Mr. Smith, representing the commission. But I am not sure, on account of his high standing at the bar, and his position generally, we would all recognize that he would take a very high stand in regard to the matter, and would assist the committee in the fullest possible way. At the same time, personally, I feel that the committee would be relieved of very much labour, and the thing would be very much more satisfactory, if we had somebody here who would assume the role of presenting the facts from the other side.
That was a very proper observation, as I said on the next page:
I am perfectly prepared to agree with everything Mr. Macdonald has said. I think he has covered the ground well.
Then the question arose as to who should name counsel for the other side. The minority of the committee submitted that as there were two sides to the inquiry, as the government was on trial and therefore naturally desired but one ending to it, as the majority on the committee being supporters of the government would naturally desire that it should be exonerated, and, as the characteristic virtue of hon. coun sel is to strive to give effect to the desire of his retainers, counsel chosen by the majority of the committee would be satisfactory neither to the minority nor to the public. On the other hand, were counsel named by the minority, it would be his duty to uphold their contention, and that of the opposition, while counsel appointed by the commissioners would uphold their contention, that of the majority and that of the government as well; so that, no interest could suffer, and both sides of the controversy would be fully presented. Now I submit to this House that that was a very reasonable and proper proposition. Lawyers know full well that the characteristic virtue of a good lawyer is to strive to carry out the desire of the man who retains him; that is inbred in the very nature of a lawyer; it is involved in the oath he takes before he begins to practice, and he cannot shake himself clear of that influence if he would, and we would not if we could. So that the proper way to get counsel in a case of this kind is for the party who is interested in reaching one conclusion to select one counsel, and the party who is interested in reaching the other conclusion to select the other counsel. The counsel selected bv those who desire to reach the one conclusion will strive to give effect to the desire of those who retain him, and the counsel appointed by the other side, as in this case the counsel appointed by the commissioners, will strive to give effect to the desire of those who retain him. It is well known to every lawyer in this House, from the right hon. the Prime Minister down to the humblest member, that that is the best wav to get. at the truth and to reach satisfactory results.
The majority of the committee having refused to adopt those well recognized principles and to allow the minority to name one of the counsel, I refused and still refuse to serve on a tribunal to hear evidence and argument adduced by counsel chosen by one side only.
The minority named counsel to whom

no reasonable objection could be taken, but the majority would not accept one of them, merely because they desired that the counsel chosen should understand that his appointment came from them, and be influenced accordingly.
It is said that the counsel chosen by the majority is able and honourable. We gladly admit that, but we deny that he is divine. Yes, he is both honourable and human, like the rest of us, and being so, he would, unconsciously, perhaps, desire to serve those who appointed him to an honourable and lucrative position. And I make that statement after an experience of many years, during which I have been associated with many of the most eminent counsel this country has ever produced, several of whom now adorn the bench of our highest courts. More than once in this country we have had eminent judges even, in special political inquiries outside of court proceedings, exercise an unconscious desire to please their political retainers.
There are many able and honourable lawyers on both sides of this House, and there is not one of them from the Prime Minister down, but knows that what I have said is absolutely true, but knows that it is absolutely unfair and contrary to public interests that counsel for both sides of this or any other question should be chosen by those on one side only interested in the result, as is being done here. There is not one who does not know that to have this investigation carried on by counsel so appointed is grossly indecent, and that the results thereof will not command the respect or confidence of the people of this country, who are fully seized of the situation.
Similar methods found great favour with the late Liberal government of Ontario shortly before its ignominious dissolution when, desirous of deceiving the people and of extricating itself from compromising positions-my hon. friend from West Peter-boro (Mr. Stratton) will recognize the facts -their modus operandi was to appoint a shrewdly selected commission of inquiry, to retain counsel of their own political persuasion to conduct it, and to refuse counsel on the other side. The results were often amusing, as well as absurd. Such an investigation in the West Elgin case produced a finding that admissions made over the signature of a Liberal member of the legislature and that of his counsel, the present Minister of Justice, were ill-founded. Another, conducted in camera, discovered that certain publishers were losing money at the prices being paid them for school books, while the facts, subsequently revealed, demonstrated that one-half those prices would yield a fair profit, and at the latter prices the books are now being supplied.
In the light of experience, I must em-Mr. CROTHERS.
phatically refuse to allow myself to be humbugged by any such transparent scheme or to be a party to any such farcical proceedings. I might add that the gentleman chosen by the four government supporters on the committee is an active politician of the Liberal type, has been a candidate for a seat in this House, and who is now conducting this investigation, figures largely in the Auditor General's report every year, and has received an average of over $3,700 per year for seven years under the present administration. In 1903-4, he received $7,800, last year he received $3,940.74, and no doubt is living in joyful anticipation of better things to come. With this gentleman conducting the prosecution against the government, with able counsel acting for the defendants, the Transcontinental Commissioners, with other able counsel representing the subordinate engineers, without any counsel appearing for the chief engineer, Mr. Lumsden, and with four impartial and righteous judges on the bench, chosen from among the political partisans of the government, who dare question the conclusion that will be reached?
Now I understand that not only are the four gentlemen who represent the government on this committee responsible for this condition of things, but that they have consulted the right hon. the Prime Minister from time to time with reference to the appointment of this counsel, and that the course they have pursued has met with his approval. There are two sides to this question. The government is responsible for the construction of this railway. It is responsible for the conduct of the chief engineer. It is also responsible for the administration by the Railway Commissioners and for the actions of every subordinate engineer who has had anything to do with that road. So that the government is vitally interested in making it appear, as the result of this investigation, that the subordinate engineers were both competent and honest. That is one side. I quite admit, as the chairman of that committee (Mr. Geoffrion) said a few moments ago, that the opposition, in this as in every case, desire to show that some blame attaches to the government. That is always the desire of the opposition. Hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition at one time, and although that was a long, time ago, it is not long enough to allow them to forget their eagerness to establish a strong case against the government then in office. It is likewise a legitimate desire on our part to show that the people are being defrauded out of large sums of money in the construction of this railway, and to bring out in the inquiry before this committee, limited though it be in its scope, limited to a very small portion of the whole road, some facts which would show how the country is being defrauded. On the other

hand, the desire of hon. gentlemen opposite is naturally to pTove if possible that everything is going on honestly and properly, and consequently they would not be likely to appoint counsel who would act vigorously in attempting to bring out the facts and prove the government guilty. Will the people be satisfied with an inquiry conducted by two counsel, both of whom were appointed by those who are particularly interested in showing there was no wrongdoing? The minority asked simply fo>-what was reasonable. They asked simply for what was granted in the case of the Me-Greevy investigation. We have had some quibbling by hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon regarding that investigation, but in substance there is no difference between the two cases. The opposition of that day were in that case making charges against the government then in office." The man who made the charges asked for the privilege of naming his own counsel. He was most interested in showing that the government were guilty of wrongdoing, and the government of that day, headed by the late Sir John Thompson, very properly acceded to his request. Mr. Tarte, who made the charges and who really represented the whole opposition, was allowed to name his own counsel, and the gentleman he retained was paid by the government. In the present instance, there is a charge made, and the House cannot get away from that. The people so understand the position. The government is responsible for the conduct of every one engaged in the construction of this great railway. The government is on trial; there is no use saying that the government is not on trial. The government desires to be exonerated and the four supporters of the government on that committee desire that the government should be exonerated. I have no objection at all to that desire; it is a very natural desire and a very legitimate desire. But, when they tell us that it is not a party matter and that they have no party feeling in it-well, they may tell that to the marines. If there is no party feeling about the matter, why did the Prime Minister not name four Conservatives instead of four Liberals on that committee? Why were four supporters of the government appointed, two of whom at least have had a great deal of experience in matters of this kind? If it is not a party matter why did the Prime Minister appoint men whom he thought would guide the inquiry to a satisfactory conclusion for the government? I do not purpose for one, Mr. Speaker, to be a party to any such farce. I have been interested in several similar investigations in the province of Ontario, and there I knew of eminent coun'r sel; counsel just as eminent as those who are engaged in this investigation-and I know what I am speaking of-deliberately
concealing documentary evidence that would be strong against the government. So that I submit, Mr. Speaker, to this House, that we were asking nothing but what was fair and reasonable, and the Conservative minority upon that committee, having been refused what was fair and reasonable, I declined to be a party to any proceeding of that kind and I am very glad that I did decline, and I would do so again under similar circumstances,

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that most hon. members who have followed this discussion have wondered why it was that my hon. friend from Simcoe precipitated a debate op this matter, and why we have lost this afternoon and this evening so far in discussing the subject he has presented to the House. Did I say subject which he has presented to the House? Perhaps I should not have used that expression, because so far as I have heard his charges, and those of his friends who have followed him, I am yet at a loss to know what subject he did present to the House. My hon. friend well knows that the proper time to discuss the facts which relate to this matter is when the committee appointed by this House makes its report after all the facts have been elicited, after all the evidence has been obtained, and when the House would be in a position intelligently, and fairly to consider the whole matter. But, the hon. gentleman did not choose to wait until then; he thought it would be a good thing for him from a political point of view to have a debate on a presentation of one side of the story. My hon. friend, and his associates have talked a good deal about this matter to-day, but they have not ventured to come in the proper parliamentary way and ask the indulgence of the House for their non-attendance on that committee. The reason is that these hon. gentlemen know they have no grounds upon which they can ask the House to excuse them for not performing their duties as members of that committee. LeT me consider for -a moment what the position of members of B parliamentary committed are. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has always manifested some regard for the maintenance of parliamentary rules, and I think that in this case he should have seen to it that his followers should pay some respect to these usages which have always obtained in this, and in the English parliament. Hon. gentlemen opposite are always ready to cite precedents from the mother country, but when it comes to their carrying out in a proper spirit the usages prevalent in the mother of parliaments, they are not very careful about their performance. When the right hon. the Prime Minister moved to appoint this committee they knew just as well as

they do to-day everything which, they have presented to the House now; they knew the committee was to be composed of a majority of members supporting the government; they knew that under the usual rules of parliamentary government a majority of that committee would be in sympathy with the government of the day, and, why did they not take the position then that they would not serve on that committee. I might suggest that there are reasons why these gentlemen have declined to serve on the committee, and these reasons may become apparent before the close of this parliament. In the meantime the reasons which they are attempting to present are not valid reasons, and do not constitute any logical argument why they should be excused from attending the committee. They went to that committee with a mandate from this House to perform a duty which the people elected them to discharge, and when they refused to perform that duty in the committee without the consent of parliament, they just as much failed in their duty to their constituents as if they had absolutely refused to sit and vote in this House. If my hon. friends want to make campaign material on a one-sided story in regard to this matter, they will no doubt be able to do so by the course they have taken.
