Mr. MAiCDONALD. And as my hon. friend from Kingston says, he is dead. Mr. Nesbitt is one of the leaders of the bar of Ontario
And a good Tory, too.

But they were de* termined not to be pleased, no matter what might be done. This only shows that my hon. friends left this committee, not because they did not have the appointment of the counsel-for they never had any warrant according to parliamentary practice or precedent for expecting any thing of the kind-but because they felt that they were in trouble, and they were looking for an excuse to get out of it. I have no desire to detain the House at greater length, because I have already talked too long, but I wanted to point out that, so far as the majority of the committee is concerned, we acceded to the proposal of the minority that counsel should be employed. We asked them to name counsel, and we discussed' with them, in the frankest way, the appointing of counsel, but they took the position that they would not accept anybody whom we might appoint, but they wanted to name the counsel themselves. We re-* plied that that was an impossible positioit for them to take, and nobody knew it better than they. I shall not trespass fur-' ther upon the time of the House. The committee is proceeding with its task to the best of its ability, and we have a counsel, Mr. Chrysler, to whom my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has referred in a manner which, on reflection, I am sure he will himself regret. Both of us belong to a profession, which is sometimes jocularly spoken of by those who do not belong to it, and we both ought to stand for its highest traditions and should be readv to recognize the merits of the best men who are in it. We who come from the smaller provinces recognize that while in some things the province of Ontario does not take the lead, it occupies, as regards the qualifications of the men who are at the head of its bar, a leading position in this Dominion; and I regretted very much .tp hear my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) talk the way he did about a gentleman occupying the position in the Ontario har which Mr. Chrysler does, and whose integrity, long experience and ability have given him a leading rank among those who are most prominent in the legal profession of that province. I do not believe that the leaders of the bar of Ontario, I do not believe that such men as Mr. Chrysler, would prostitute their abilities to the achievement of some petty advantage in party politics. I believe that Mr. Chrysler will bring out in this investigation whatever facts it is possible to bring to light. I am sorry that my hon. friends opposite have formed so low an estimate of the duties of the gentlemen who compose a committee such as this. If there be any duty of importance in this House, it is that devolving upon the members of a commit-

tee of investigation to look into the matters at issue with the greatest possible care, and bring out all the facts to the light of day. True, we all have oiir party predilections, 'but I would be sorry to think that any one in this House would be willing to sacrifice his ideas as to what is right and proper in order to gain a miserable poltical advantage. On behalf of the majority of this committee. I submit that we are endeavouring to carry out the task allotted to us to the best of our ability, and with the sincere desire that, if there be any wrongdoing, it may be brought to light. Who cares, from a political point of view, if there have been engineers, who, out in the northern wilds, have made wrong classifications?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

A good many of them are friends of hon. gentlemen opposite. Do they mean to say that the position of this government will be affected in the slightest degree if it be shown that a certain resident engineer somewhere in northern Ontario has wrongly classified common excavation as rock cutting. The desire of this government, I take it, is that, if there be anything of the kind, it should be shown, and that if any engineers have been guilty of wrongdoing, they should be dismissed at once.

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Macdonald) may congratulate himself on the ingenuity with which he evaded a great number of questions put to him by this side. Some of them he evaded by a method he has cultivated for many years, and others he evaded by answers, the transparency of which are only too apparent to every member of this House. Still others he evaded by promising to reply later on and then forgetting to do so. More than once in his speech I asked him, after he had said that the prosecutor was Mr. Lumsden, to be good enough to tell the House who the prosecuted was.
If my hon. friend ' will permit, what is it he would like to know?
I do not know why the hon. member rose, if he does not understand what I want to know.

I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) was asking me a question in the course of the remarks I was making-and I intimated that I would speak to the point-as to the persons who were charged in this case.
The hon. member stated who the prosecutor was in the investigation. I asked, who was the prosecuted?

So far as appears from the reference to the committee, Mr. Mr. E. M. MACDONALD.
Lumsden stated that he had lost confidence in certain of the engineers. He has given us the names of these engineers, and certain information in regard to the conduct which caused him to lose confidence in them. I should imagine that among the people against whom the charges are made are these engineers. In his statement, Mr. Lumsden made no reflection at all upon the commissioners.

The hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) having stated that the prosecutor was Mr. Lumsden was, in logic, compelled to say that the prosecuted was the engineers. _ If it was possible for this House to bring itself to such a conclusion as that, we may, with patience, listen to the arguments of hon. members opposite. If a committee of this House is to be appointed at the suggestion of the Prime Minister to investigate a point in dispute between one employee of a public commission, and those employed under him, then, as I say, we may possibly listen with patience to the argument. But I do not understand that the status of a committee of investigation of this House is merely to inquire into a quarrel between certain employees of the government. If this came down to a mere dispute concerning classifications between Mr. Lumsden, and his sub-engineers, I should say that the proper parties to investigate were the parties regularly appointed by the authority of this House, and not a special committee appointed at the suggestion of the Prime Minister. Surely, we can trust Mr. Lumsden to investigate questions of lack of skill, or care, on the part of the employees under him; we need no committee of this House to look into such matters as that. I would like the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) to give this House a precedent for the appointment of a committee of this House to investigate a quarrel between civil servants of the government. If the government are not implicated, if members of this House are not implicated, where is the precedent for the appointment of such a committee? There was a commission appointed by this House-not a committee of this House, but a commission from outside-to investigate the Civil Service. This is one commission-let me say in answer to the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. A. H. Clarke)-that members on this side do not consider a farce. The precedent of appointing a commission of that sort has not been repeated by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I venture to say never will be. But to say that a committee of seven members of this House are to sit at a cost of $1,000 a day merely to dis~ cuss the merits of a quarrel between an engineer and his sub-engineer, the facts of which do not go beyond these officers, is to talk what I must regard-and what every man in this country will regard-as arrant

nonsense. There can be no question, and the people of the country, so conceive it, that the prosecutors in this case are those concerned in the success of the investigation, those represented by the opposition in this House, and that the parties defendant in this case are the commission appointed by the government, and through them the government itself. You may cloud the issue as you like, but that is how it is regarded in the country, and.no man who wants to be fair, and to talk common sense will say anything else. We must consider that the parties who are charged-by whom they are charged may be another question-and who are in the position of defendants, are the Transcontinental Railway Commission, and through them the government, because on no other basis can logic or common sense be claimed for the appointment of a committee of this House to investigate.
Another question that the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) did not answer is this: Why did he and his confederates on that committee decline to accept the counsel nominated by the opposition members there? He knows better than to try to answer that question. Should he give the first answer that might occur to him, he would say that this gentleman was not competent counsel. But, were he to say that, he would 'be laughed at. The country would say: Cannot we trust those whose political fortunes are bound up with the success of the investigation to appoint the most competent counsel they can find? Were the hon. member to answer that this gentleman -was not a Liberal, he would be laughed to scorn; if he were to say that he was a Conservative, the error would be equally apparent. So, the hon. member cannot answer the question, and until he answers it to the people of this country he cannot defend the position of the committee or show that they were anxious to have a thoroughly useful investigation.
Now, if the hon. gentleman even appeared to make a point in the whole course of his speech, it was when he said that he could not find, in the course of British or Canadian history, a precedent for any powers whatever devolving upon the minority of a committee. Now. I had not intended to take part in this discussion, when it opened, consequently I have not had time to look up precedents. Only one precedent has been mentioned on either side of the House in this debate; there is only one parallel case brought to the attention of the House; and, if there is one thing clearer than another emerging from this discussion, it is that that precedent is absolutely on the side of the members of the opposition. Some years ago, a committee of investigation was appointed by this House to consider certain charges against members of the House. On what side were 194
the people in that investigation? It was to the interest of the people that these charges be thoroughly probed. The people were represented by Mr. Tarte, a member of this House. The interests of the people were analogous to the interests of Mr. Tarte; the two were inseparably bound up. When Mr. Tarte appointed his counsel, that counsel was necessarily counsel for the people. Now, Mr. Tarte in that case, occupied a position exactly similar to the minority of the committee in the case now before us. The party concerned with the success of the investigation, the party analogous to the prosecution, were represented by Mr. Tarte. The party analogous to the defence were represented by those in this House charged by Mr. Tarte. Both had counsel in that case; only one had counsel in this case. Who are the parties in the present case identified with the success of the prosecution? Who are the parties in this case whose political fortunes, to an extent at all events, are bound up with the thoroughness of the investigation? Why, the opposition members of the committee. Yet, there is absolutely no counsel to represent them. There cannot possibly be counsel to represent the people. On the other hand, the members of the Transcontinental Commission and the government are arm in arm with counsel, they are surrounded with counsel at every point. Mr. Smith is counsel for the commission, he is counsel for the defence, he is also counsel for the government. Then there are the four counsel on the committee, there is the counsel who represents the contractors, and the contractors are interested in securing the very same verdict that the four members of that committee are interested in securing; consequently the counsel who represents the contractors is also arm in arm with the government. There is also the counsel for the sub-engineers, I understand that there was one there to represent them, and he is arm in arm with the government too, because the only verdict of that committee that can possibly suit the engineers is the very verdict that will suit the government members of the committee. All these counsel are retained to secure one end, and one alone, they are all working for the same goal, they cannot be otherwise true to their clients. And now, as if to heap injury on insult, they appoint Mr. Chrysler, who is the nominee of the four government members, and who, to put it in the fairest possible way, is not concerned solely to secure a successful and useful result to that investigation.
Now, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat complained bitterly that we on the opposition side of the House have had so much to say of the enormous cost of the Transcontinental railway. I sympathize with that hon. gentleman. I can understand that he, as a member of the



government party, a3 well as every other member of the government party will always be seriously alarmed whenever this question of the cost of the Transcontinental railway comes up. It appears to get worse as time goes on, and I do not think the people can hear too often of what has taken place, and of what is taking place in regard to the construction of that railway, when there is an addition to the cost of one hundred millions, an addition sufficient to take care of the public works of this country for years to come, an addition to the cost of a sum of mon.ey that equals $12 or $13 for every man, woman, and child in Canada, an addition to the cost that is accounted for by only one of two things, either by worthless and fraudulent estimates given by the government, or their engineers when the matter was first entered upon, or by the worthless, and fraudulent classification which has taken place in the interest of the contractors, and through them perhaps in the interest of others. Now, the situation is surely serious enough to demand a serious investigation; and whether there were a precedent or not in British or Canadian history, if the members of that committee were really desirous of prosecuting these charges with a view of ascertaining the cause of this enormous increase, it was their duty to pay no attention whatever to precedent, but to take their position on the side of the people, to coincide with the wishes of the opposition. I affirm that there is no man in this country, if he will put aside for the moment party considerations, so foolish as to say that the interests of any prosecution, or of any defence are best conducted when they are not most closely identified with those interested in securing the success and thoroughness of that investigation. It was a matter of minor consideration whether there were precedents or not, the end to be attained was the great consideration, and as I said before, every principle of common sense, every principle of law should have led every member of that committee to place himself in unison with the principle that you could not too closely identify the conduct of an inquiry with those interested in securing its success.
Now, Sir, I want to refer to a matter which, although I must confess is not absolutely in point of the discussion, still it serves the purpose of bringing before this country the direct association of this government with the wrongs of the Transcontinental railway. I want to point out two or three things before I sit down. In 1903 this House, in its wisdom, laid down a plan whereby this matter of over-classification was to be investigated, and decided upon, they laid down the plan of arbitration free and untrammelled, and to a large extent they determined that that Mr. MEIGHEN
plan should be followed in the event of dispute. They placed very few limits on the method of arbitration, or on the manner of it. But we had the spectacle some four years afterwards of the Minister of Railways, and the Transcontinental Commission conspiring together to limit the methods adopted by this House for conducting that arbitration. The Transcontinental Railway Commission, on the 10th of January, 1908, of their own motion, deliberately set to work to confine within limits which this House never contemplated, the powers of that Arbitration Board. The Minister of Railways, when this matter was under discussion last fall, admitted on the floor of parliament that he was a party to that alteration, and that it was done at his instance. By the way, Sir, my experience has led me to this conviction, that whenever a speaker in this House reaches the proud position of attacking the Minister of Railways, that hon. gentleman will be found engaged in a forced sleep, because I have always observed that when a discussion is unusually hot, that ig the attitude which the Minister of Railways assumes. Now, not only did he by that memorandum, limit the method, and limit the principle of arbitration as they had been laid down by this House in 1903, but for two long years that commission, which should have represented the people of this country, and guarded their interests, were struggling with the officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific to enforce that unwarrantable limitation of the Arbitration Board; for two long years, during which the evidence was dying out, during which witnesses were disappearing, during which the evidence that could have been adduced earlier was being wiped away by time, for two long years that struggle went on, the Grand Trunk Pacific on the one hand struggling with the Transcontinental railway Commission for the full and free investigation as determined and outlined by this House, and the Transcontinental Commission struggling pertinaciously on the other side. Now, was not that a melancholy spectacle? Is not that something for the people to consider, that those who were appointed to guard their interests, were struggling against their interests, and against the intent and meaning of an Act of parliament?
Not only were they doing so, but they were doing so with the tacit and expressed approval of the Minister of Railways and Canals himself. The struggle went on unceasingly and bitterly, and it did not end until, by the union of the skill of the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works some change suddenly came ovef the scene. There is only one thing unexplained by the report brought down in connection with that struggle. One thing not explained is that we find that when

the angelic presence of one member of the government, the Minister of Public Works, floated over the scene, peace suddenly ensued. He seemed to have the effect of the twin stars, as celebrated* by Horace, on the stormy sea. The winds fell, the waves were stilled and the turbulence that surged over the waters existed no longer. Why that was it is impossible to conceive, but we must remember, in trying to reach a solution, that there was one way of appeasing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway 'Company. There was a method of appeasing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company that must appear to any one who thoroughly studies that report. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company appear in a double capacity. They appear in the capacity, in the first place of lessors of the road later on and as such interested in its cost, but they are also in the capacity of contractors on many portions of the line. In one capacity they are interested, to a 3 per cent extent, in keeping down the cost, and in the other capacity they are just as interested in keeping up the cost. In seeking for an explanation of the sudden peace that came over the storm we must remember that. It is only right to remember that. It does* not show a suspicious* mind; it only shows mat a very possible explanation is to be found there. Whether it existed or not we do not know. The fault I find with the government is that they have refused such an investigation as would ascertain what the real cause was. They confined it within limits that were absurd, and that is the charge which they must answer for before the people of this country. Had they assisted in an investigation that might have been useful within its terms we might have been able to trace the connection, if there were any, between the ills that were perpetrated in the construction of this road and the government which was in charge supposedly on behalf of the people. The hon. mem: her for South Essex (Mr. Clarke) closed his speech with a homily on the difference between a quitter and a server. I could not help but think that he was more anxious to bring in a joke about the white feathers that he saw on a crest than to teach any useful lesson to the House. But . if one has to decide whether he is going to be a quitter or a server he should first of all come to a decision as to what he is quitting and what he is serving. There is no essential virtue in quitting and there is no essential virtue in serving. I have no doubt_ that if a man should decide to quit serving mammon he would do well, and the hon. member for South Essex ought to have given consideration to the question as to whether he was serving mammon upon that committee rather than talk about the crests that he saw upon the walls 194J
of the committee room. I cannot see what' object could possibly have been served by the members of the opposition further remaining there. That committee was a farce and it had no other motive from its very birth. As soon as that was abundantly plain what could these hon. gentlemen do but withdraw from the committee? What purpose could they serve by wasting their energies on the committee any longer?' The only thing that might have resulted was that they might have been identified' with a report, the farcial character of whicli is as certain as anything could be certain in any parliament, and there would be no one more surprised than the members of that committee and myself if that report does not absolve the engineers, the commission and the government, just as it was intended to absolve them when the committee was first appointed.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara).
speechtext:
I did not intend to take any part in this discussion, but there are some propositions set forth by hon. gentlemen opposite, regarding the duties of members of parliament, that I wish shortly to protest against in so far as I am concerned, so that I will not be understood as in any way assenting to them by my silence. The hon. member for Pictou" (Mr. Macdonald) for instance, in the course of his speech, while referring, as a justification of the position of the majority of this committee, to the historical Larkin-Connolly investigation in regard to money that was stolen, or alleged to have been stolen, prior to 1891, declined to answer what I thought was a very pertinent question in regard to the matter that he was then discussing, as to whether the charges made by Mr. Tarte were in the interest of the people. He evaded that answer, but the answer is manifest that unless Mr. Tarte was a hypocrite and a humbug, the charges were made in the interest of the people. The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was in the House at that time, and he got the full benefit of those charges. They helped to get him into power, because they hammered into this country and among the people the idea that the conduct of the Public Works Department was a sample of the administration of the government at that time. He was assisted to take that position because of the uncompromising and absolute honesty of the Minister of Justice of that day, Sir yJohn Thompson, who insisted upon cleaning up what was wrong, whether it was done by Conservative or Liberal. The Minister of Justice of that day was a Minister of Justice in fact as well as in name, and it made no difference to him where the charges came from. He saw to it that when wrong was done, whether by Conservatives or Liberals, it was punished and the whole

force of the government was turned in to probe those wrongs and see that justice was done, not for the Conservative party, not for the Liberal party, but for the people of this great country. The Prime Minister today owes a great- deal of his success in getting into power in 1896 to the fact that the Minister of Justice of that day was that kind of a man, and saw that charges, when made, were prosecuted to their utmost in the interest of the people. Yet, the hon. member for Pictou declined to tell me whether Mr. Tarte made these charges in the interest of the people. I say that he did. I was not in the House at that time, but I know something about that investigation, because some of the people most concerned lived in the city of St. Catharines. A great many of the witnesses concerned in the case lived in St. Catharines, in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and I know that witnesses were brought here and that witnesses who tried to escape were forced to come here by virtue of the Dominion police, through the action of Sir John Thompson, to prove the charges, if they could prove them, no matter whose ox was gored, and no matter what party suffered. I say again that the Prime Minister, to a great extent, achieved power by virtue of the conduct of Sir John Thompson, and because of his determination that if charges were made they should be probed, and that if wrong existed, it must be stopped. The hon. member for Pictou attempted to justify the action they have taken in declining to appoint counsel, as suggested by the minority, and I am not here concerned in saying whether the minority or the majority should have the appointment of counsel, but I say that the Prime Minister, who controls every committee of this House, and who has the say as to who shall conduct these investigations, ought to do like Sir John Thompson did, and see that counsel is appointed in the interest of the people.
Notwithstanding the very eloquent argument of the member for Pictou, it is idle for the Prime Minister to pretend that any one is to-day representing the people of Canada in that investigation. Applying the precedent in the McGreevy-Connolly investigation, as there is no counsel to-day appointed by the person who is making the charges as was the case in that investigation, then the government should see to it that a public prosecutor is appointed. Supposing somebody iays an information charging some one or other with a serious crime, and the person who lays the information declines to engage a counsel, is the government to say that because he will not do so, they are not concerned about it? Is not the government the guardian of the public morals of this country? Is the Prime Minister unconcerned about how much money has been stolen on the Mr. LANCASTER.
Transcontinental railway,	because-Mr. Lumsden contending that he appears only as a witness-will not take the responsibility of naming counsel? Is the Prime Minister absolutely indifferent as to whether Mr. Lumsden's charges are substantially true or not? Is not the Prime Minister the chief trustee of the affairs of the people of this country, and, if his Minister of Justice will not do his duty, and if the members of the committee will not take the right view, is it not his duty to declare that counsel will be appointed to represent the people? In my humble opinion the Prime Minister is to blame if that investigation is not properly conducted in the interests of the people of Canada. Is this House to be turned into a two-penny-halfpenny court of inquiry to determine a row between engineers in the employ of the government; is there not a far greater principle at stake in this matter? If the superintendent of the Welland canal charges a subordinate with not doing his duty, is a committee of this House to be appointed, and an inquiry instituted at an expense of $1,200 a day to determine such a petty question as that? And yet, it is to such a trivial issue that the Prime Minister would limit this Lumsden inquiry. All the Prime Minister has to do is to put his Anger on the button and he can secure that the rights of the people in this matter are properly protected. In my humble opinion the Prime Minister is guilty of dereliction of duty if after what he has heard today he does not appoint counsel to represent the people of Canada to prosecute thege charges. When Sir John Thompson was Minister of Justice a different course was taken by him, and that course was approved b,y the Liberal party then in opposition. Is it to 'be said that a course which the Prime Minister approved of before he assumed office is now to be repudiated by him? I rose, Sir, to enter mv protest against such conduct on the part of the Prime Minister and his government, and having done so, I can say no more.
I presume, the purpose having been served, the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) will consent to withdraw his motion?	>

Yes, Mr. Speaker ; it was in deference to what you said that I moved the motion.
Motion (Mr. Lennox) withdrawn.

The Minister of Railways promised some time ago that he would investigate the Clarry matter. Has he any information to give with reference to thatS I have subpoenaed Mr. Clarry to the Public Accounts Committee to-morrow, and I

*would like to know whether the minister will assist me in the prosecution-I mean the investigation.
My hon. friend is more anxious for other people to assist him in the prosecution than he is to assist other people.	.
I should have said investigation.

I sent a member of my staff with full authority to investigate under oath the charges made by the hon. member for Simcoe, or rather the charges contained in documents which he read to the House. I had hoped to have the report of that official to-day, but at all events, I think I shall have it to-morrow or on Monday.

The minister stated that Mr. Clarry would be paid on the first of April. I have drawn attention to certain facts in connection with Mr. Clarry which, as I am instructed would render it not proper to pay him at present. Does the minister propose to pay him on the first of April?

Mr. Clarry is an official of the Department of Justice and not of my department. I imagine that the inquiry must have referred at least incidentally to Mr. Clarry, and if the report shows that Mr. Clarry is innocent of wrongdoing, I see no reason why he should not be paid. However, as to the matter of payi ment, the Minister of Justice, in whose employ he was, will deal with that.
I was told that the investigation did not include Mr. Clarry.
Incidentally it did, I think.
We are going on with the investigation to-morrow.
I cannot control that.
Better not pay the money.
Is there any particular significance in paying him on the first of April?
Except that the suggestion came from the hon. member (Mr. Lennox).
It was the minister who said he would pay him on the first of April, and I thought the suggestion was rather unfortunate.
House again in committee to consider the proposed resolution of Sir Frederick Borden to amend the Militia Pension Act.

Since last evening I have looked into this matter more
carefully, and I find that the amendment which was proposed by my hon. friend from Centre York (Mr. Wallace) will not be necessary, for the reason that subsection (e) of 6B will include the only officer who would be affected by that amendment, Under this subsection he will be able to count sufficient time to become eligible for a pension within the age limit to which he will be able to serve on the permanent corps. Therefore, I have asked my hon. friend not to press his amendment, because I think it undesirable to legislate for one individual, particularly when it is not necessary. The case is a meritorious one, and I have told my hon. friend that if it should turn out that I am not correct in this, I shall be glad myself to introduce the amendment which he has suggested next session. My hon. friend has accepted this statement on my part. Otherwise I think the resolution was fully considered.

This resolution deals somewhat with the South African contingent. I mentioned to the minister that there were a few cases of hardship that have not yet been dealt with by the government. I refer to the relatives of those who started for South Africa, and died on the way. The legal representatives of those who reached Suuth Africa, and died there have participated in the grants of land made by the government, while the relatives of those who died on the way have received nothing. There are only a few of these cases, and I think the minister or the government should provide for them. I know that these people feel that they have been harshly treated, and I think some action should be taken to put the matter right.

I am glad my hon. friend has brought the matter up, but I think he will agree with me that the grievance to which he refers cannot be dealt with in this Bill, which is merely for the purpose of amending the Militia Pension Law. It would have to be dealt with by an amendment to the Act providing land grants for South African veterans. While I cannot give any promise, I have told my hon. friend that I will be glad to consider the matter.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 194) to amend the Militia Pension Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved second reading of Bill (No. 180) to amend the
60iHI

Royal Military College Act. He said: From time to time, o-wing to the growth of the Royal Military College, the amount of money necessary to pay salaries has been increased. I think there have been amendments on three different occasions. Now it is proposed to amend the Act so that the limit shall be $60,000 a year instead of $30,000 a year. I explained that the commandant is being paid a larger salary than his predecessor because, owing to the adoption of the plan of creating a general staff throughout the empire, it is desirable to have an officer at the Royal Military College holding the highest class in the army; and to get such a man, you must pay more.
